Applications are filed on the DMVA scholarship portal, not with the college.
records.agency: North Carolina Department of Military and Veterans Affairs

records.title: Burial in a North Carolina State Veterans Cemetery
records.summary: North Carolina provides a free burial plot and interment services in a state Veterans cemetery for a qualified Veteran. A spouse and certain dependents can be buried there too, but a burial fee applies to them.
records.amount: No charge for the gravesite or necessary interment services for a qualified Veteran. A burial fee applies for an eligible spouse or family member.
eligibility: Any former member of the US Armed Forces who served on active duty and was discharged under honorable conditions
A Veteran entitled to retired pay for non-regular service in the Reserve Components or the Army or Air National Guard, or who would be entitled but for being under 60 years of age
The spouse, widow, or widower of a qualified Veteran
Unmarried minor children under 21, or under 23 if enrolled in an approved course of education
An unmarried adult child who became permanently disabled before age 18
details: The state covers the burial plot, opening and closing the grave, the marker and its installation, and perpetual care for a qualified Veteran.
All funeral expenses stay the responsibility of the Veteran, the family, or the estate.

The DD Form 214 is the primary document used to verify honorable service. Reserve and National Guard members claiming eligibility through non-regular service present a 20 year letter or proof of retired pay eligibility.
If you cannot find your DD-214, a county or state Veterans service officer can help you get a replacement copy.
records.agency: North Carolina Department of Military and Veterans Affairs

records.title: North Carolina State Veterans Homes skilled nursing care
records.summary: North Carolina runs State Veterans Homes that provide skilled nursing care, therapy, and on-site help from Veterans Service Officers. The homes are state licensed and approved for Medicare, Medicaid, and third party insurance.
eligibility: The state page does not publish the admission requirements. Call the department or a Veterans Service Officer to find out whether you qualify and what the cost would be.
details: The department lists State Veterans Homes at Black Mountain, Fayetteville, Kernersville, Kinston, and Salisbury.
Care is provided by registered nurses, licensed practical nurses, and certified nursing assistants under the direction of licensed physicians, with a registered dietician and social work support.
Physical, occupational, and speech therapy are provided in the facility, along with therapeutic recreation programs and community outings.
Veterans Service Officers work on site and help residents apply for VA benefits.
Hospital care is arranged through VA medical centers or local hospitals.
The department lists a toll free number, 844-624-8387, to reach a Veterans Service Officer.
records.agency: North Carolina Department of Military and Veterans Affairs

records.title: Veterans preference in North Carolina state government employment
records.summary: North Carolina gives eligible Veterans a hiring preference for state jobs covered by the State Human Resources Act. Military training and additional service count toward the qualifications for the job.
eligibility: A Veteran who served during a period of war
A Veteran with a service-connected disability incurred during peacetime
The spouse of a disabled Veteran
A surviving spouse or dependent of a Veteran who died on active duty during a period of war as a result of that service
Surviving family members of a Veteran who died for service-related reasons during peacetime
details: The preference applies to positions subject to the State Human Resources Act with every state department, agency, and institution. It reaches initial employment as well as promotions, reassignments, and horizontal transfers.

The State Human Resources Commission must give an eligible Veteran credit for all military service training or schooling that relates to the requirements of the job, plus experience credit for additional military service once the minimum qualifications are met.
Some categories of positions are excluded. Check N.C.G.S. 126-83 for the exclusions before you count on the preference for a specific posting.
records.agency: North Carolina Office of State Human Resources

records.title: Alternative veterans property tax exemption
records.summary: New York's main property tax break for wartime Veterans. It takes a percentage off the assessed value of your primary residence, with extra credit if you served in a combat zone or have a service-connected disability rating.
records.amount: 15 percent of assessed value for wartime service, plus 10 percent more for combat zone service, plus an amount equal to half your VA disability rating times the assessed value. Each part is capped, and the caps vary by locality.
eligibility: You served in the active military, naval, space, or air service during a period of war, or you received an armed forces, navy, marine corps, or global war on terrorism expeditionary medal

You were discharged or released under honorable conditions, or you have a qualifying condition or are a discharged LGBT Veteran as defined in section one of the veterans' services law, which covers Veterans discharged over sexual orientation or gender identity
The statute's qualified owner is a Veteran, the spouse of a Veteran, or the unremarried surviving spouse of a Veteran
The property must be used exclusively for residential purposes and be the primary residence of the Veteran or unremarried surviving spouse
Your county, city, town, village, or school district must have opted in. Each level of government decides separately
details: The statute sets three layers. The basic layer is 15 percent of assessed value. Combat theatre or combat zone service, documented by a United States campaign ribbon, service medal, or expeditionary medal, adds another 10 percent. A compensation rating from VA or the Department of Defense for a service-connected disability adds the assessed value multiplied by 50 percent of the disability rating.

Each layer is capped at the LESSER of a dollar figure or that figure multiplied by the latest state equalization rate for your assessing unit. The figures are $12,000 for the basic layer, $8,000 for the combat layer, and $40,000 for the disability layer. A locality may also adopt a local law reducing the maximum, so ask your assessor what applies to your parcel.
Someone who served during a period of war and died in service of a service-connected disability is deemed to have a 100 percent compensation rating for the disability layer.

The war periods listed in the statute are the Spanish-American war, the Mexican border period, World War I, World War II, Korea, Vietnam, and the Persian Gulf conflict from 2 August 1990. The Persian Gulf period has no end date in the statute, so later service still counts.

Being away from the home for medical reasons or because you are institutionalized does not cost you the exemption. If part of the property is used for something other than residence, only that part is taxed.

Where more than one qualified owner owns the property, their exemptions may be combined. A Veteran who is also the unremarried surviving spouse of a Veteran may claim what the deceased spouse was entitled to as well.
This exemption does not apply to special district charges.

It is not automatic. File an application with your local assessor by your municipality's taxable status date. Tax.ny.gov gives 1 March as the usual date and tells you to confirm it with your own assessor.
You can only receive one of New York's three long-standing Veteran exemptions: this one, the Cold War exemption under Real Property Tax Law 458-b, or the eligible funds exemption under section 458.

Separately, a new full exemption for permanently and totally disabled Veterans starts with taxable status dates on or after 1 October 2026. See that record. It is a local option and the statute says it is in addition to other exemptions.
records.agency: Your local assessor, with guidance from the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance

records.title: Veterans credits on New York civil service examinations
records.summary: New York adds points to your civil service exam score if you are a Veteran, and more points if you are a disabled Veteran. You can use the credit only once in your civil service career.
records.amount: Disabled Veterans: 10 points on an original appointment exam and 5 points on a promotion exam. Other Veterans: 5 points on an original appointment exam and 2.5 points on a promotion exam.
eligibility: For the non-disabled Veteran credit: you are an armed forces member with an honorable discharge or discharge under honorable circumstances, including Veterans discharged over sexual orientation or gender identity who qualify under the statute
You are a U.S. citizen or permanent resident and a New York resident at the time of application

For the disabled Veteran credit: the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs or a military department certifies that you are entitled to disability payments for a service-connected disability rated at 10 percent or more
The credit is one time. Once you receive a permanent original appointment or a permanent promotion using the credit, you cannot claim it again
details: The statute reads that a disabled Veteran gets "ten points additional in a competitive examination for original appointment" and "five points additional credit in a competitive examination for promotion." A non-disabled Veteran gets "five points additional credit in a competitive examination for original appointment" and "two and one-half points additional credit in a competitive examination for promotion."
If an appointment is terminated during the probationary period, you keep your eligibility for credits on future exams.
The credit is added only after you pass the exam. You have to claim it, so watch for the veterans credit question on the exam application.
records.agency: New York State Department of Civil Service, and local civil service commissions

records.title: Reduced fee hunting, fishing, and trapping licenses for disabled Veterans
records.summary: New York resident Veterans with a service-connected disability rating of 40 percent or more pay a reduced fee for a hunting, fishing, or trapping license, get free bowhunting and muzzleloading privileges, and get preference for Deer Management Permits.
records.amount: $5 for your first hunting, fishing, or trapping license of the year, per the DEC page. Additional licenses that same year are free, and bowhunting and muzzleloading privileges are free with a base hunting license.
eligibility: You are a New York State resident
You have a service-related disability of 40 percent or more
You provide a letter from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs with your case number stating that your service-related disability is 40 percent or more
For hunting or trapping, you also need a hunter education certificate or a previous license
You need proof of New York State residency
details: DEC states that once you provide the VA letter and your eligibility is recorded in your license file, you will not need to provide that letter again. After that first verification at a license issuing agent, you can buy licenses online, by phone at 1-866-933-2257, or at an agent location.
Note that the Department of Veterans' Services page describes annual proof from the VA, while the DEC page describes a one time letter. Confirm what your license issuing agent needs before you go.
Disabled Veterans also get preference in the Deer Management Permit selection.

A separate Patriot Plan benefit gives free hunting, fishing, and trapping licenses to qualifying active service members, including New York National Guard and U.S. Reserve members, and lets nonresident military members stationed in New York for more than 30 days buy at resident prices.
records.agency: New York State Department of Environmental Conservation

records.title: Eligible funds veterans property tax exemption
records.summary: An older New York property tax exemption for property bought with military pension, bonus, insurance, or prisoner of war compensation money. The exemption is tied to how much of that money went into the property.
records.amount: No more than $7,500 of exemption per individual's military or naval service, per the statute.
eligibility: The property was purchased with the proceeds of eligible funds

The statute defines eligible funds as "pension, bonus or insurance, or dividends or refunds on such insurance, or payments received as prisoner of war compensation from the United States government", granted by the United States or by New York for military or naval services
Eligible claimants include the person who rendered the service, and also a spouse, unremarried surviving spouse, dependent father or mother, or children under age 21
You must file a verified application with your assessor on or before the taxable status date, showing the amount of eligible funds used toward the purchase
details: The exemption tracks the amount of eligible funds actually used to buy the property, rounded to the nearest multiple of fifty dollars. The statute caps it: "no such exemption on account of eligible funds paid on account of military or naval services rendered by an individual shall be allowed in excess of seven thousand five hundred dollars."
Mixing eligible funds with other money, or the government holding some of it back for insurance premiums, does not disqualify you. The statute says so directly.

Unlike the alternative exemption, this one applies to state, county, and general municipal taxation without the locality opting in. A school district has to adopt a local law before it applies to school taxes.

The $7,500 ceiling has one exception. Under subdivision 5, a locality may adopt a local law that adjusts the exemption up or down by the change in level of assessment factor after a revaluation, so the amount can move.

That same local law may let owners who previously had this exemption, but switched to the alternative exemption under section 458-a, switch back. If you gave this up years ago, it is worth asking your assessor whether your municipality adopted it.
This exemption does not apply to special district charges.

You can only receive one of New York's three long-standing Veteran exemptions: this one, the alternative exemption under 458-a, or the Cold War exemption under 458-b. Ask your assessor which leaves you better off before you switch.
records.agency: Your local assessor, with guidance from the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance

records.title: MERIT Scholarship for families of service members killed or severely disabled
records.summary: The Military Enhanced Recognition Incentive and Tribute scholarship pays the cost of attendance for children, spouses, and financial dependents of New York service members who died, went missing, or became severely and permanently disabled in the line of duty.
records.amount: Cost of attendance, not to exceed the average cost of attendance charged to New York resident students at a state-operated SUNY college.
eligibility: The service member died as a result of injury or illness suffered or incurred while performing military duties, is classified as missing in action, or became severely and permanently disabled from injury or illness incurred in service
The service member was a New York State resident at the time of death or disability
You are the child, spouse, or financial dependent of that service member. A severely and permanently disabled service member may also apply on their own behalf
You are a U.S. citizen or eligible noncitizen
You have a high school diploma or GED
You are enrolled full time, defined as at least 12 credits per term
details: Coverage runs 2 years for an associate degree, 4 years for a bachelor's degree, and 5 years for an approved five-year program.

Apply by completing the FAFSA and the New York State TAP application first, then submitting the MERIT Scholarship application through the web supplement along with the required documentation, including a disability verification form where applicable.
HESC lists the application as open year round.
This covers members of the United States Armed Forces and the New York State organized militia.
records.agency: New York State Higher Education Services Corporation

records.title: New York income tax treatment of military pay and military pensions
records.summary: New York does not tax military pension payments at all. Active duty pay is taxed based on your residency, and combat zone pay is excluded.
records.amount: Military pensions are fully exempt from New York State, New York City, and Yonkers income taxes.
eligibility: Military pension: the Tax Department states that "Military pension payments you receive as a retired military personnel or as their beneficiary are totally exempt from New York State, New York City, and Yonkers income taxes"

Residents: active duty pay is taxed to the same extent as federally, except that combat zone pay is not taxed, and neither is compensation or bonus pay for active service while a prisoner of war or missing in action during the Vietnam conflict
Nonresidents: the Tax Department states that "your military pay is not subject to New York State income tax"
Part-year residents: only military pay earned while you were a New York resident is taxable

Nonresident military spouses: income earned in New York is excluded from New York source income under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act and exempt from personal income tax, if you are a nonresident in New York solely to be with a service member spouse who is here on orders
details: The pension exemption reaches the beneficiary of a retired service member, not only the retiree.
Veterans' benefits such as tuition payments and subsistence allowances are treated the same as federally. If they are excluded from your federal gross income, New York does not tax them either.
A nonresident claims the exclusion through subtraction modification S-119 on Form IT-225. Your military pay may also be exempt from New York withholding.

The nonresident spouse exemption covers wages and salary for work done in New York and business income from a sole proprietorship or partnership carried on here. It keeps applying if your service member spouse is later assigned to another state or overseas and you stay.

Members of the New York State organized militia, which is the New York Army National Guard, Air National Guard, Naval Militia, and New York Guard, can subtract pay for active service performed within New York State under state active-duty orders issued under Military Law section 6.1, or under federal Title 10 active-duty orders for service other than training. Pay for regular duties, such as the annual two week training, does not qualify.

A reservist called to active duty, or a regular member, may be able to defer payment of back income taxes by showing that military service materially impaired the ability to pay. You must already have a notice of tax due or an installment agreement.
This entry covers state tax treatment only. Federal tax treatment is separate.
records.agency: New York State Department of Taxation and Finance

records.title: Full property tax exemption for a permanently and totally disabled Veteran, starting October 2026
records.summary: New York has created a new exemption that takes your primary residence off the property tax roll entirely, including special district charges, if VA considers you permanently and totally disabled from military service. It is a local option and it starts with taxable status dates on or after 1 October 2026.
records.amount: A full exemption of the primary residence from taxation and from special district charges, assessments, and special ad valorem levies.
eligibility: The VA considers you permanently and totally disabled as a result of military service, shown by a letter, official form, or other VA document that says so specifically

And you were discharged or released under honorable conditions from active military, naval, space, or air service, including Army and Air National Guard service performed under federal Title 10 orders
Or you have a qualifying condition as defined in section one of the veterans' services law, and your discharge was something other than bad conduct or dishonorable
Or you are a discharged LGBT Veteran as defined in section one of the veterans' services law, and your discharge was something other than bad conduct or dishonorable
You meet all the other requirements of Real Property Tax Law 458-a, including that the property is your primary residence
Your county, city, town, village, or school district has adopted a local law or resolution offering it
details: This is new law. It was enacted as Real Property Tax Law 458-a(11) by L.2025 ch.672 and amended by L.2026 ch.59 Part EE and ch.77. The Tax Department says it applies to assessment rolls based on taxable status dates occurring on or after 1 October 2026.
As of this writing the Tax Department has not yet posted the application form or instructions. It says they are in process and will appear on the veterans exemptions page at tax.ny.gov.
It is a local option, so it only exists where your county, city, town, village, or school district has adopted it. Each of those decides separately.

There is a way to check rather than guess. Every locality that adopts it must notify the New York State Department of Veterans' Services within thirty days, and that department has to keep a publicly available record of which ones have. Ask them, or your assessor.

The statute says this exemption is in addition to other Veteran exemptions under this chapter, and specifically that it does not require giving up an exemption under section 458(3). That is different from the older three exemptions, where you may only hold one.
It cannot reduce your taxable assessed value below zero.
Unlike the alternative and eligible funds exemptions, this one does reach special district charges, assessments, and special ad valorem levies.
records.agency: Your local assessor, with guidance from the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance

records.title: Service-Disabled Veteran-Owned Business certification
records.summary: New York certifies businesses majority owned and controlled by service-disabled Veterans, which opens access to state contracting opportunities and a public directory that state agencies use to find vendors.
eligibility: One or more service-disabled Veterans with "a service-connected disability rating of 10% or more" from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs own at least 51 percent of the business
Service-disabled Veteran ownership must be "real, substantial, and continuing"
The Veteran owner or owners must have and exercise authority to independently control day-to-day business decisions
The business must qualify as a small business, which OGS states means no more than 300 employees
The business must be "located in New York State or have a significant business presence in New York State"
details: The program is authorized under Article 3 of the Veterans' Services Law, per the Office of General Services.

Apply online in four steps: create a NY.GOV Business Account through the Service-Disabled Veterans' Enterprise System, log in, complete the Business, Applicant, and Financial Information sections, then review, attest, sign electronically, and submit.
Certified businesses are listed in the state's public SDVOB directory. Certification must be renewed through a recertification process.
The Division of Service-Disabled Veterans' Business Development can be reached at 518-474-2015.
records.agency: New York State Office of General Services, Division of Service-Disabled Veterans' Business Development

records.title: New York State Veterans Homes skilled nursing care
records.summary: New York runs five skilled nursing homes for Veterans. Eligible Veterans get skilled nursing and rehabilitative care, and the state says there is no means test or income limitation for the benefit.
eligibility: You need skilled nursing care
You "entered active duty from the State of New York or be a New York State resident for one year prior to application"
You had an honorable discharge from the U.S. Armed Forces
You had at least 30 days of active service
Spouses of qualified Veterans may also be admitted if they were married at least one year and require skilled nursing care
Admission is subject to bed availability
details: The five homes are at St. Albans in Jamaica, Batavia, Oxford, Montrose, and Long Island in Stony Brook.

The Department of Veterans' Services page states that "There are no out-of-pocket costs charged to the Veteran residing in a State Veterans Home for routine skilled nursing care" and that "This benefit has no means test or income limitation." It also states that the Veteran keeps all Social Security, pension, and other income that would normally be applied against long term care costs.

On the federal share, the page states that "For a Veteran with a service connected disability rating at 70% or greater, the Department of Veterans Affairs will pay State Veterans Homes the full cost to provide skilled nursing to that Veteran (38 U.S.C. 1745)."

Confirm current cost and payment arrangements with the admissions office at the specific home before you rely on them. Phone numbers listed by the state are St. Albans 718-990-0353, Batavia 585-345-2049, Oxford 607-843-3121, Montrose 914-788-6000, and Long Island 631-444-8387.
records.agency: New York State Department of Veterans' Services, with the homes operated through the State University of New York and the Department of Health

records.title: Vehicle registration and plate fee exemption for certain Veterans
records.summary: New York waives registration and plate fees for Veterans who received a vehicle through the federal Title 38 automobile grant, and for Veterans who qualify for Medal of Honor or Former Prisoner of War plates.
eligibility: You are a Veteran with disabilities who received a motor vehicle under Federal Title 38, the federal automobiles and adaptive equipment program for certain disabled Veterans and members of the Armed Forces
Or you qualify for and apply for Congressional Medal of Honor custom plates
Or you qualify for and apply for Former Prisoner of War custom plates
details: Eligible Veterans are exempt from both registration fees and vehicle plate fees.

For the Title 38 exemption, DMV asks for form MV-1E, the Statement to Register a Vehicle Under Title 38, along with a copy of VA Form 21-4502, the VA approved application for an automobile. DMV states the exemption covers one vehicle, which must be a passenger car, suburban, or light truck under 20,000 pounds.
Military and Veteran custom plates are ordered on form CP-30. Former POW and Congressional Medal of Honor plates use form MV-1H.

Separately, DMV extends driver license validity for active duty members for up to 6 months after discharge or separation, and allows renewal of an expired license within two years after discharge if no more than 30 months have passed since discharge.
The New York State Department of Veterans' Services Benefits Advisor line is 1-888-838-7697.
records.agency: New York State Department of Motor Vehicles

records.title: New York State Veterans Tuition Award
records.summary: A state tuition award for New York resident Veterans attending an approved degree or vocational program. It is pegged to SUNY resident undergraduate tuition rather than a fixed dollar figure.
records.amount: The annual undergraduate resident tuition rate at a SUNY state-operated campus, or your actual tuition, whichever is less. Part-time awards are prorated by credit hour.
eligibility: You are a U.S. citizen or eligible noncitizen
You are a legal resident of New York State and have resided in New York State for 12 continuous months
You were discharged under honorable conditions
You have at least four years of active duty service, or you served in combat in Vietnam, the Persian Gulf, or Afghanistan
National Guard members qualify with four or more years of active duty deployment, or with certain expeditionary medals

HESC lists qualifying service as Vietnam service from November 1, 1955 to May 7, 1975, Persian Gulf service on or after August 2, 1990, and Afghanistan service during hostilities on or after September 11, 2001, or receipt of an Armed Forces Expeditionary Medal or equivalent
details: The award cannot exceed undergraduate tuition at a state-operated SUNY campus, so a private school award will not cover the full bill.

For a degree program, file the FAFSA and the New York State TAP application first, then submit the Veterans Tuition Award application. For vocational training, submit the Veterans Tuition Award application and HESC will email a separate payment application if you are eligible.
HESC lists the deadline as open year round. Award duration is limited and depends on whether you are in a vocational program or a degree program.
HESC's phone number is 1-888-NYSHESC, which is 1-888-697-4372.
records.agency: New York State Higher Education Services Corporation

records.title: Veterans Credit on Ohio Competitive Civil Service Examinations
records.summary: Ohio adds a percentage credit to a Veteran's score on competitive civil service examinations for state and local government jobs. Reserve and national guard members who finished initial entry level training get a smaller credit.
records.amount: Ohio Revised Code 124.23 provides additional credit of twenty per cent of the person's total grade given in the examination for a qualifying honorably discharged Veteran, and fifteen per cent for a qualifying reserve component or Ohio national guard member. The two cannot be combined.
eligibility: Twenty per cent credit: completed service in the uniformed services and received an honorable discharge, or was transferred to the reserves with evidence of satisfactory service. Must be a resident of the state.
Fifteen per cent credit: member of a reserve component, including the Ohio national guard, who has completed initial entry level training.
Must be a United States citizen or have legally declared the intent to become one.
Must receive a passing grade on the examination before any additional credit is applied.
details: The credit is applied on top of a passing score. It does not turn a failing exam into a passing one.
The twenty per cent and fifteen per cent credits cannot be stacked.

The text of 124.23 examined here does not extend this exam credit to disabled Veterans as a separate larger credit, or to surviving spouses. If you have seen a claim that it does, verify it against the current statute before relying on it.

Ohio Revised Code 5903.11 separately requires state agencies running federally funded employment and training programs to operate a Veteran priority system, referring special disabled Veterans first, then Vietnam era Veterans, then disabled Veterans, then all other Veterans.
records.agency: Ohio Department of Administrative Services and local civil service commissions

records.title: Ohio County Veterans Service Commissions: Local Emergency Aid and Claims Help
records.summary: Every Ohio county has a Veterans service commission funded by county property tax dollars. It employs accredited service officers who file VA claims at no charge and it can award direct emergency financial assistance for rent, utilities, food, and other needs. This is one of the strongest county level Veteran systems in the country.
records.amount: Funding comes from a county levy that Ohio Revised Code 5901.11 caps at not to exceed five-tenths of a mill per dollar on the assessed value of the property of the county. Individual assistance awards are set by each commission, so there is no statewide dollar figure.
eligibility: Ohio Revised Code 5901.08 opens assistance to a veteran, an active-duty member of the armed forces of the United States, or the spouse, surviving spouse, dependent parent, minor child, or ward of such a person.
The applicant must have been a resident of the county for at least three months.
Section 5901.09 requires a statement of household income and property, so awards are needs based.
details: Each commission has five members appointed by the judges of the court of common pleas. Members must be honorably discharged or honorably separated Veterans, and the seats represent the major Veterans organizations.

Section 5901.06 lets the commission employ an executive director, investigators, and clerks. Section 5901.07 covers county Veterans service officers and assistants. These service officers help you file and appeal VA claims and they do not charge for it.

Section 5901.15 provides for immediate assistance and establishes a Veterans service commission unclaimed assistance fund, which is the path for urgent needs that cannot wait for the regular meeting cycle.
Commissions also fund transportation to VA medical appointments, burial of indigent Veterans, headstones, and cemetery plot maintenance under the later sections of Chapter 5901.

Because funding and allowance schedules are set county by county, what is available in Cuyahoga County is not the same as what is available in Vinton County. Go to the commission in the county where you live.
records.agency: County veterans service commission in your county of residence

records.title: Ohio Disabled Veteran License Plates and Registration Fee Exemption
records.summary: A qualifying disabled Veteran can register one vehicle in Ohio without paying the registration fee or service fee, and is exempt from local motor vehicle taxes and the transfer fee on that vehicle. The plate itself is red, white, and blue and carries the word veteran.
records.amount: For the first vehicle registered, Ohio Revised Code 4503.41 states a disabled veteran is not required to pay any registration fee and service fee, and exempts that registration from local motor vehicle taxes and transfer fees. Additional vehicles beyond the first are charged normally.
eligibility: Awarded funds under the Disabled Veterans' and Servicemen's Automobile Assistance Act of 1970 because of a service-connected disability, or
Has a service-connected disability rated or compensated at one hundred per cent by the veterans' administration.
details: The plate is red, white, and blue, bears the word veteran, and is imprinted with the international wheelchair symbol.
The fee exemption is limited to the first vehicle. Registering a second or third vehicle with the plate does not carry the exemption.

Ohio issues several other military and Veteran plate types under Chapter 4503, including Purple Heart and other award plates. Those have their own qualifying documents and their own fee treatment, so check each one separately with the BMV rather than assuming the 4503.41 exemption carries over.
Holding a special Veteran license plate issued by the registrar of motor vehicles also opens the door to free hunting and fishing licenses under Ohio Revised Code 1533.12.
records.agency: Ohio Bureau of Motor Vehicles, registrar of motor vehicles and deputy registrars

records.title: Enhanced Homestead Exemption for Disabled Veterans and Surviving Spouses
records.summary: Ohio gives a disabled Veteran a larger homestead exemption than the standard senior exemption. It shields a set amount of the true value of the Veteran's owner-occupied home from property taxation, and a qualifying surviving spouse can keep it after the Veteran dies.
records.amount: Ohio Revised Code 323.152 sets the disabled Veteran reduction at fifty thousand dollars of the true value of the property in money, as adjusted each year. That is double the twenty-five thousand dollar figure used for the standard senior and disability homestead reduction.
eligibility: Veteran of the armed forces of the United States, including reserve components, or of the national guard, discharged or released from active duty under honorable conditions.

Has received a total disability rating, or a total disability rating for compensation based on individual unemployability, for a service-connected disability or combination of service-connected disabilities as prescribed in Title 38, Part 4 of the Code of Federal Regulations.
Owns and occupies the homestead. The reduction applies to only one homestead owned and occupied by a disabled Veteran.

A surviving spouse who occupied the homestead when the disabled Veteran died and who acquires ownership of the homestead may continue the reduction. It continues through the tax year in which the surviving spouse dies or remarries.
details: Ohio Revised Code 323.151 carries the definitions of disabled veteran and surviving spouse of a disabled veteran that control this exemption.

The fifty thousand dollar figure is indexed, and the statute says exactly how. Each September the tax commissioner takes the percentage increase in the gross domestic product deflator published by the federal Bureau of Economic Analysis over the preceding calendar year, applies it, and rounds to the nearest one hundred dollars. The commissioner then certifies the new amount to every county auditor no later than 1 December, and it applies to the following tax year. Ask your county auditor for the figure in force.
The commissioner does not make the adjustment in a year when it would produce a figure lower than the current one, so the amount does not fall.

A surviving spouse who occupied the homestead when the disabled Veteran died and who acquires ownership may continue the reduction. It runs from the year the Veteran dies, or where the rating came after death, from the first year on 1 January of which the total disability rating had been received for the deceased spouse. It continues through the tax year in which the surviving spouse dies or remarries.
A surviving spouse can also qualify where the Veteran died before receiving the disability rating, if that person otherwise met the disabled Veteran definition and owned and occupied the homestead.
The reduction is in lieu of the other homestead reductions, not on top of them, and it applies to only one homestead.
The same statute provides a separate reduction, also fifty thousand dollars of true value, for the surviving spouse of a public service officer killed in the line of duty.

The exemption works as a reduction in taxable value, not a check. The statute multiplies the fifty thousand dollars by the assessment percentage, which cannot exceed 35 percent, and by the effective tax rate for your property, so the dollar benefit differs by county and district.
records.agency: County auditor of the county where the homestead is located, under rules of the Ohio Department of Taxation

records.title: Free Ohio Hunting and Fishing Licenses for Disabled Veterans and Military
records.summary: Ohio issues hunting and fishing licenses, permits, and stamps free of charge to permanently and totally disabled Veterans, former prisoners of war, and Veterans holding special military license plates. Active duty members on leave can hunt and fish without a license, with limits.
records.amount: Free of charge. Ohio Revised Code 1533.12 lets the chief of the division of wildlife issue these free licenses, permits, and stamps on an annual, multi-year, or lifetime basis as the chief determines appropriate.
eligibility: Veterans with a service-connected disability rated permanently and totally disabling by the Veterans Administration, who receive compensation and were discharged under honorable conditions.
Honorably discharged former prisoners of war.
Veterans issued a special license plate by the registrar of motor vehicles qualify for the same free licenses and permits as disabled Veterans.
Every resident of a state or county institution, charitable institution, or military home in this state is issued an annual fishing license free of charge.

Active duty members on leave or furlough may fish, hunt wild birds and wild quadrupeds, and trap fur-bearing animals without a license or fur taker permit, if they carry military identification and follow Ohio's game laws.
details: The active duty leave exception is not unlimited. Deer and wild turkey hunting still require the applicable permits.
All of these require proper application through the state procedures the division of wildlife sets, so the license is free but not automatic.
The statute does not set a fee schedule for these Veterans. It removes the fee, so the question at the counter is proof of eligibility, not price.
records.agency: Ohio Department of Natural Resources, Division of Wildlife

records.title: How and When to Apply for the Ohio Homestead Exemption
records.summary: The homestead exemption is not automatic. The owner files an application with the county auditor on a form supplied by the tax commissioner. Ohio Revised Code 323.153 sets the filing deadline and also allows a late application for the prior tax year.
eligibility: The owner of the homestead files the application, for the tax year in which the reduction is sought.
details: File with the county auditor of the county in which the homestead is located.
The application uses a form devised and supplied by the tax commissioner, which asks only for information needed to establish eligibility and the amount of the reduction.
The statute states the application shall be filed on or before the thirty-first day of December of the year for which the reduction is sought.
A manufactured or mobile home is the exception. Those applications must be filed in the year before the year you want the reduction for.
Once an application is approved it is a continuing application. You do not refile every year, and the auditor treats the absence of a new application as evidence you are still entitled.

Late filing is contemplated. You may file a late application for the preceding tax year alongside the current year application. If the auditor finds it correct, they work out what you would have received had you filed on time, and that amount is refunded to you as an overpayment of taxes under Ohio Revised Code 5715.22.

If you stop qualifying in a later year, you have to tell the county auditor. The statute says that conviction for willfully falsifying information to get the reduction, or failing to give that notice, revokes your right to the reduction for three years.
The application also requires you to affirm that you did not acquire the home from a relative, other than your spouse, in order to qualify for the reduction.
records.agency: County auditor, Ohio Department of Taxation

records.title: Ohio Burial at Public Expense for Indigent Veterans and Family
records.summary: When an Ohio Veteran dies without the means to pay for a funeral, the county pays for burial or cremation through the Veterans service commission. The same protection extends to a Veteran's spouse, surviving spouse, and parent.
records.amount: Ohio Revised Code 5901.25 directs that the arrangement be made at a fair and reasonable price. The section reviewed here does not state a maximum dollar allowance, and county commissions set their own schedules, so ask your county Veterans service commission for its current allowance.
eligibility: A Veteran who dies without the means to defray the necessary funeral or cremation expenses.
The parent of a Veteran, the spouse of a Veteran, or the surviving spouse of a Veteran, who dies without those means.
details: The board of county commissioners requires the Veterans service commission to contract for the service and to cause the person to be interred or cremated at public expense.
Chapter 5901 also covers grave markers, headstones, and maintenance of Veterans' cemetery plots in its later sections.

This is separate from federal burial benefits. A Veteran may also be eligible for burial in a national cemetery, a government headstone or marker, and a VA burial allowance. Ask the county Veterans service officer to check both tracks.
Contact the county Veterans service commission before making funeral arrangements. Approval processes generally run through the commission, not the funeral home alone.
records.agency: County veterans service commission and the board of county commissioners

records.title: Ohio Income Tax Deduction for Military Retirement Pay and Active Duty Pay
records.summary: Ohio lets a taxpayer subtract military retired pay from Ohio adjusted gross income, so uniformed services retirement is effectively not taxed by the state. A separate deduction covers active duty pay for servicemembers stationed outside Ohio.
records.amount: The retirement deduction is not capped by a dollar figure in the statute. It removes the qualifying retired personnel pay from Ohio adjusted gross income to the extent it was included in federal adjusted gross income and not already deducted or excluded.
eligibility: Retired pay deduction: amounts received as retired personnel pay for service in the uniformed services or reserve components thereof, or the national guard.
The retired pay deduction also reaches amounts received by the surviving spouse or former spouse of such a taxpayer under the Survivor Benefit Plan on account of that taxpayer's death.

It also reaches federal civil service retirement. If you draw a CSRS or FERS pension that is based in whole or in part on credit for your uniformed service, you may deduct the portion attributable to that service.

Active duty pay deduction: military pay and allowances received for active duty service in the armed forces, reserve components, or the national guard. The deduction may not be claimed for military pay and allowances received while the taxpayer is stationed in this state.
details: The retired pay deduction is Ohio Revised Code 5747.01 division (A)(23). The active duty pay deduction is division (A)(21) and turns on where you are stationed, not on residency alone.

The federal civil service part is the one people miss. A Veteran who bought back military time toward a CSRS or FERS pension can deduct the share of that pension attributable to uniformed service, so long as it is in federal adjusted gross income and not already deducted.

You cannot take this deduction on an amount you also claimed the Ohio retirement income credit on under Ohio Revised Code 5747.055, and an amount deducted here does not count toward adjusted gross income for that credit.
Two more deductions sit right beside these in the same statute. Division (A)(24) covers payments from the Ohio military injury relief fund, and division (A)(25) covers the Ohio veterans bonus.
All of these are deductions taken in computing Ohio adjusted gross income, so they are claimed on the Ohio return rather than through a separate application.
VA disability compensation is not part of this. It is already excluded from federal adjusted gross income, so there is nothing to deduct.
records.agency: Ohio Department of Taxation

records.title: Ohio Credit for Military Training Toward Occupational Licenses
records.summary: Ohio licensing agencies must count military training and service experience toward the education and experience requirements for a professional license when that training is substantially equivalent to the civilian standard. Related sections protect licenses during active duty.
eligibility: Applicants for an Ohio occupational or professional license whose military training or service experience is substantially equivalent to or exceeds the licensing standard.
Licensees called to active duty who need a renewal accommodation or a continuing education extension.
details: Ohio Revised Code 5903.03 requires licensing agencies to accept military training and service experience as satisfying education and experience requirements where it is substantially equivalent to or exceeds the standard for the license.
Section 5903.10 addresses renewal of a license or certificate for servicemembers.

Section 5903.12 lets a licensee called to active duty extend the continuing education reporting period by the number of months served on active duty, and 5903.121 covers factors used in determining fulfillment of required continuing education.

Chapter 5903 also carries reinstatement and reemployment rights in section 5903.02, giving the same rights as federal law with exclusive jurisdiction in the courts of common pleas, and preferential hiring policy authority in section 5903.15.

Each licensing board applies this in its own rules. What counts as substantially equivalent is a board by board determination, so submit your DD-214, training records, and any credentialing transcripts to the specific board.
records.agency: The individual Ohio occupational licensing board or agency

records.title: Ohio Veterans Homes: State Long Term and Nursing Care
records.summary: Ohio operates state Veterans homes providing long term and nursing care to eligible Ohio Veterans. Residents are charged based on ability to pay rather than a fixed market rate, and the statute caps what can be assessed.
records.amount: There is no flat charge in the statute. Residents may be assessed based on ability to pay, and the assessment shall not exceed the difference between the total per diem amount collected by the state and the average annual per diem cost for the resident's maintenance.
eligibility: Served honorably during a conflict period as determined by the United States Department of Veterans Affairs, or received specified military medals.
Meets the citizenship requirement and has one year of Ohio residency.
Is disabled by disease, wounds, or otherwise, and is incapable of earning a living.
Excluded: a person whose mental condition causes the person to be dangerous to the community.
details: The homes are governed by the Director of Veterans Services within the Ohio Department of Veterans Services, with a superintendent appointed by the director running each facility day to day.
Chapter 5907 names a facility in Sandusky, which houses The Robert T. Secrest Nursing Home.
Of the resident fees collected, the statute directs eighty per cent to operations and twenty per cent to capital improvements.
County Veterans service commissions may provide transportation assistance to and from the homes.

Bed availability, current per diem figures, and the memory care and domiciliary options are not in the statute. Contact the Ohio Department of Veterans Services or your county Veterans service office for the current admission packet.
records.agency: Ohio Department of Veterans Services, Director of Veterans Services

records.title: Ohio War Orphans and Severely Disabled Veterans' Children Scholarship
records.summary: Ohio helps pay college costs for the children of Veterans who died or who carry a severe service-connected disability. At Ohio state-supported colleges and universities the award takes the form of an exemption from general and instructional fees, with a grant option at private and career schools.
records.amount: Two forms of award under Chapter 5910: exemption from general and instructional fees at state-supported colleges, or a grant equal to the average scholarship value for students at private institutions or career colleges. Capped at five academic years at the undergraduate level.
eligibility: Child of a Veteran who died, or of a Veteran with a sixty per cent or greater service-connected disability, or of a Veteran receiving benefits for permanent and total nonservice-connected disability, as determined by the United States Department of Veterans Affairs.
The parent served in the armed forces of the United States during a conflict period specified in the chapter. Certain U.S. Merchant Marine service also counts.

Age at application: Ohio Revised Code 5910.03 requires the applicant to have attained the sixteenth, but not the twenty-fifth, birthday. For children of prisoners of war or those missing in action the window is narrower: has attained the sixteenth, but not the twenty-first, birthday.

Residency: if the Veteran entered service as an Ohio resident, the applicant must have lived in Ohio for the preceding year. If the Veteran was not an Ohio resident at entry, the applicant must have resided in Ohio for the year before application plus any four of the last ten years.
The scholarship board determines financial necessity.
details: Administered by the Ohio War Orphans and Severely Disabled Veterans' Children Scholarship Board: the chancellor of higher education, the director of veterans services, one state representative, one state senator, and four appointees from the American Legion, VFW, Disabled American Veterans, and AMVETS.
The award covers general and instructional fees. It is not a full cost of attendance award, so room, board, books, and other fees are generally the family's responsibility.

Application deadlines are set administratively by the Ohio Department of Higher Education and are not in the statute. Check the current deadline with the department or with your county Veterans service office before the term you want covered.
records.agency: Ohio War Orphans and Severely Disabled Veterans' Children Scholarship Board, Ohio Department of Higher Education

records.title: Amputee and Paralyzed Veterans Pension
records.summary: Pennsylvania pays a state pension to a Veteran who lost, or lost the use of, two or more extremities because of a service-connected injury or disease. It is paid on top of other Commonwealth and federal assistance.
records.amount: $150 per month, in addition to other Commonwealth and federal assistance
eligibility: Was a Pennsylvania resident upon entering military service and listed the Commonwealth as the residence on enlistment
Honorable or Under Honorable Conditions discharge. A dishonorable discharge disqualifies the applicant
A service-connected injury or disease resulted in the loss, or the permanent and severe or complete paralysis, of two or more limbs
At least a 40 percent disability compensation rating in each of the affected limbs, as certified by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs
details: The Adjutant General determines eligibility and issues the implementing regulations.
You apply through the County Director of Veterans Affairs in the county where you live.
DMVA lists the documents that speed processing: a copy of the DD214, proof of Pennsylvania residency at entry into military service, and the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs decision letter.
DMVA cites 51 Pa. Consolidated Statutes Chapter 77 and 43 Pa. Code Chapter 5 as the legal authority.
General questions go to RA-MVVeteransPension@pa.gov. Completed applications and personal information should not be emailed.
records.agency: Pennsylvania Department of Military and Veterans Affairs

records.title: Blind Veterans Pension
records.summary: Pennsylvania pays a state pension to a Veteran whose service-connected injury or disease caused blindness. The statute says it is paid in addition to any other assistance the Veteran receives from the Commonwealth or the federal government.
records.amount: $150 per month, in addition to other Commonwealth and federal assistance
eligibility: Was a resident of Pennsylvania upon entering military service and listed Pennsylvania as the residence on enlistment
Honorable or Under Honorable Conditions discharge. A dishonorable discharge disqualifies the applicant
A service-connected injury or disease resulted in loss of vision
Visual acuity with correcting lenses of 3/60 or 10/200 or the equivalent, or less, in the better eye, or the visual field of the better eye is contracted to not greater than 20 degrees
details: The Adjutant General determines eligibility and the decision is final under the statute.
You apply through the County Director of Veterans Affairs in the county where you live.
DMVA lists the documents that speed processing: a copy of the DD214, proof of Pennsylvania residency at entry into military service, and the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs decision letter.
General questions go to RA-MVVeteransPension@pa.gov. Completed applications and personal information should not be emailed.
records.agency: Pennsylvania Department of Military and Veterans Affairs

records.title: Free and reduced-fee fishing licenses for disabled Veterans
records.summary: A Pennsylvania resident Veteran rated 100 percent service-connected disabled can get a free disabled Veteran lifetime fishing license. A Veteran rated 60 to 99 percent can get a resident fishing license at a reduced fee set by statute at $1.
records.amount: Free lifetime fishing license at a 100 percent rating, plus a free Combination Trout and Lake Erie Permit. The statute sets the license at $1 for a 60 to 99 percent rating.
eligibility: Pennsylvania resident
Service-connected disability certified by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs
Free lifetime license: rated 100 percent disabled by the VA
Reduced-fee license: rated 60 to 99 percent disabled by the VA
A former prisoner of war certified by the appropriate branch of the armed forces may also obtain a resident fishing license for $1 under the same statute
details: The Fish and Boat Commission states that a Veteran who qualifies for the free license is also issued a Combination Trout and Lake Erie Permit free of charge.
The first license must be obtained in person from a county treasurer, the Fish and Boat Commission's Harrisburg office, or one of the six regional law enforcement offices.

Bring proof of Pennsylvania residency, such as a driver license or other documentation of domicile, and written certification from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs confirming the service-connected disability rating.
After the first verification, annual renewals can be obtained from any issuing agent or online at huntfish.pa.gov.
records.agency: Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission, and county treasurers

records.title: Free and reduced-fee hunting and furtaker licenses for disabled Veterans
records.summary: A Pennsylvania resident Veteran whose wartime disability includes the loss or loss of use of a limb, or who is rated 100 percent disabled by the VA, gets a free hunting or furtaking license. Veterans rated 60 to 99 percent get one at a reduced fee.
records.amount: No charge for the resident disabled Veteran hunting and furtaker licenses. For a 60 to 99 percent rating the statute sets a $1 license. The Game Commission publishes the reduced disabled Veteran hunting and furtaker license at $2.97.
eligibility: Pennsylvania resident who is a Veteran of a war or armed conflict, with a service-incurred disability

Free license: the disability consists of the loss of one or more limbs, or the loss of the use of one or more limbs, or the Veteran is 100 percent disabled as certified by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs
Reduced-fee license: a disability rating between 60 and 99 percent as certified by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs
The applicant must otherwise qualify and be mentally and physically fit to hunt
The application must state that the applicant is a war or armed conflict Veteran and that the qualifying disability was service incurred
details: You apply to the Game Commission or to a county treasurer. The issuing agent or the Commission may require the applicant's discharge papers.

A Veteran whose qualifying disability is permanent may obtain a lifetime license. The Game Commission lists the resident disabled Veteran lifetime hunting and furtaker licenses, and their renewals, at no charge, and says the lifetime licenses are issued through county treasurers only.
The Game Commission lists a disabled Veteran license replacement at $6.97.
A former prisoner of war may buy a resident hunting license for $1 plus the current issuing fee under the same statute. The Game Commission publishes the prisoner of war hunting license at $2.97.
The Game Commission also publishes resident military, National Guard, and reserves hunting licenses at $2.97.
records.agency: Pennsylvania Game Commission, and county treasurers

records.title: Disabled Veterans Real Estate Tax Exemption
records.summary: Pennsylvania can exempt a Veteran's principal residence from real estate tax if the VA rates the Veteran 100 percent permanently disabled, unemployable, blind, paraplegic, or as having lost two or more limbs, and the State Veterans' Commission finds financial need.
records.amount: Full exemption from real estate tax on the principal dwelling. There is no partial or scaled exemption.
eligibility: Pennsylvania resident with an Honorable or Under Honorable Conditions discharge from the U.S. Armed Forces
Served during a period of war as determined by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs. DMVA says operation-specific or service-specific expeditionary medals can also establish wartime service

Has one of the following from the VA: 100 percent permanent service-connected disability, total disability individual unemployability, service-connected blindness, paraplegia, or loss of two or more limbs
The property is the principal dwelling and is owned solely by the Veteran, jointly with a spouse, or as an estate by the entirety
The State Veterans' Commission must determine that the Veteran has financial need
An unmarried surviving spouse may continue to receive the exemption if the Commission determines need
details: The need test works off a published income level, and there is one right answer rather than two. The statute at 51 Pa.C.S. 8904 set the original rebuttable presumption at $75,000 and requires the State Veterans' Commission to adjust it every two years by the change in the Consumer Price Index. The adjusted figure is published in the Pennsylvania Bulletin.

The current figure is $114,637, effective 1 January 2025. The Commission set it in a notice at 55 Pa.B. 149, published 4 January 2025, applying a 6.1 percent rise in the Northeast all items CPI-U over the two years from 1 November 2022 to 31 October 2024. The previous level was $108,046. Adjustments have been made in 2009, 2011, 2013, 2015, 2017, 2019, 2021, 2023 and 2025, so the next one is due 1 January 2027.
That Pennsylvania Bulletin notice is the thing to check, not a county page. One notice every two years covers this figure.

If your household income is above the presumptive level you are not disqualified. You can request a full determination of need under 43 Pa. Code 5.24(d), and you qualify if your allowable monthly expenses exceed your monthly household income. Expenses must be documented, and the calculation includes a cost of living allowance and counts the potential real estate tax itself as an expense.
If you were denied for need before 1 January 2025, DMVA specifically encourages reapplying under the higher level. The effective date runs from the date of the new application.
You apply through the County Director of Veterans Affairs in the county where you live, not directly to the state.

Under the statute the county assessment board grants the exemption once the State Veterans' Commission certifies eligibility, and the Commission reviews exemptions periodically. Denials may be appealed to the Adjutant General.
DMVA asks that general questions go to Ra-retx@pa.gov, and that completed applications and personal information not be sent by email.
records.agency: Pennsylvania Department of Military and Veterans Affairs, with the State Veterans' Commission and county assessment offices

records.title: Educational Gratuity Program for children of disabled or deceased Veterans
records.summary: Pennsylvania pays a per-semester gratuity directly to an approved Pennsylvania school for the child of a wartime Veteran who is rated 100 percent permanently and totally disabled or who died in service or from a service-connected disability.
records.amount: Up to $500 per term or semester per qualified child, paid directly to the approved educational institution. Payments run no longer than four scholastic years, which DMVA describes as eight payments.
eligibility: The child is between 16 and 23 years of age. The statute allows payments to continue past 23 if the child is still completing the course of study
The child has lived in Pennsylvania for the five years immediately before applying
The child attends an approved educational institution located in Pennsylvania
The child demonstrates financial need

The Veteran parent had an Honorable or Under Honorable Conditions discharge and served during a period of war or armed conflict, and is rated 100 percent permanent and total service-connected disabled by the VA
Alternatively, the Veteran parent died in service during a period of war or armed conflict, or died as a result of a service-connected disability
details: The money goes to the school, not to the student or the family.
DMVA lists the documents to bring: the Veteran's DD214 or military death certificate, the applicant's birth certificate, photo identification, and proof of five years of Pennsylvania residency.
You apply through the County Director of Veterans Affairs in the county where you live.
The statute lets the department adjust the per-term amount to stay within the appropriation, so the payment can be less than the maximum.
DMVA points applicants to the VA WEAMS tool to check whether a Pennsylvania school is approved. General questions go to Ra-eg@pa.gov, and personal information should not be emailed.
records.agency: Pennsylvania Department of Military and Veterans Affairs

records.title: How Pennsylvania taxes military pay and military retired pay
records.summary: Pennsylvania does not tax federal active duty pay earned outside the state, and does not tax military retired or retainer pay. Military service performed inside Pennsylvania by a Pennsylvania resident is generally taxable compensation.
records.amount: Retired or retainer pay is exempt from PA personal income tax. Active duty pay earned outside Pennsylvania is not taxable. Active duty pay for service performed inside Pennsylvania is taxable, with a narrow emergency exception.
eligibility: You are a Pennsylvania resident filing a PA personal income tax return
For the out-of-state exclusion, the pay must be for federal active duty or federal active duty for training performed outside Pennsylvania
details: The Department of Revenue states that military pay received while on federal active duty or federal active duty for training outside Pennsylvania is not taxable. Leave it off Line 1a of the PA-40 and attach copies of your W-2 and your military orders with an explanation of the amount excluded. Revenue says it will not process the return without proof the pay was earned outside Pennsylvania.

Income received by a Pennsylvania resident for military service performed inside Pennsylvania is taxable even on federal active duty or active duty for training, unless it is active military duty within Pennsylvania for an emergency under 35 Pa.C.S. Ch. 76.

Reservists and National Guard members ordered to active duty for training under Title 10 or Title 32 are on federal active duty, so the same inside and outside rule applies. Compensation for weekend drills performed inside Pennsylvania remains taxable.

The PA Personal Income Tax Guide states that "Retired or retainer pay of a member or former member of a uniform service calculated under Chapter 71 of Title 10, U.S. Code as amended" is exempt from PA personal income tax.

The same guide excludes from taxable compensation "amounts received as a disability pension, disability annuity, or similar allowance for physical injuries or sickness resulting from active service in the armed forces of the United States."

Watch the Tax Forgiveness trap. Revenue says military pay that you correctly left off the PA-40 should still be included in eligibility income for Tax Forgiveness. Only hazardous duty pay and pay earned in a combat zone are left out of eligibility income.

A Pennsylvania resident serving in a combat zone or qualified hazardous duty area gets the same extension as federally, automatically extended to 180 days from the last day of service or the last day of continuous hospitalization for an injury incurred there. Print COMBAT ZONE at the top of the return and include a copy of your orders.
records.agency: Pennsylvania Department of Revenue

records.title: Pennsylvania Veterans Homes long-term care admission
records.summary: Pennsylvania runs six state Veterans Homes offering long-term care. Veterans, their spouses, and surviving spouses may apply. Residents pay a monthly maintenance fee set according to their ability to pay.
eligibility: Served in the U.S. Armed Forces or the Pennsylvania Military Forces and was discharged under honorable conditions
Had Pennsylvania as the home of record upon entry into military service, or is a bona fide Pennsylvania resident. Current Pennsylvania residents receive priority in admissions
Spouses of eligible Veterans and surviving spouses of eligible Veterans may also apply
details: The six homes are the Delaware Valley Veterans' Home in Philadelphia County, the Gino J. Merli Veterans' Center in Lackawanna County, the Hollidaysburg Veterans' Home in Blair County, the Pennsylvania Soldiers' and Sailors' Home in Erie County, the Southeastern Veterans' Center in Chester County, and the Southwestern Veterans' Center in Allegheny County.
A resident makes monthly payments against maintenance fee liability in accordance with the resident's ability to pay.
Admissions are first come, first served, and an admissions committee determines the level of care needed. A decision may be appealed.

DMVA lists conditions that make an applicant ineligible, including a need for mental health care or custody, behavior that threatens the applicant or others, a need for treatment the home cannot provide, unresolved alcoholism or substance abuse, contagious disease, and a felony conviction unless the applicant shows good character and has been conviction-free for at least five years after incarceration.
The homes state that they provide varying levels of care, so confirm which level a specific home offers before applying.
records.agency: Pennsylvania Department of Military and Veterans Affairs

records.title: Free vehicle registration and Veterans designation on a PA driver license
records.summary: PennDOT waives registration and title fees on one vehicle for Veterans in several specific categories, including Purple Heart and Medal of Honor recipients and former prisoners of war. Pennsylvania also lets a Veteran add a Veterans designation to a driver license.
records.amount: Registration and title fees are waived on one passenger vehicle or truck weighing 9,000 pounds or less. License plate fees still apply.
eligibility: Lost a limb, lost an eye, or became partially paralyzed while serving in the U.S. Armed Forces
Was captured by the enemy in an armed conflict for which the Department of Defense authorizes a campaign medal
Was awarded the Congressional Medal of Honor
Was awarded the Purple Heart
details: The waiver covers one passenger vehicle or truck of 9,000 pounds or less. Plate fees are not waived.
The application is PennDOT form MV-371DV, which carries the full eligibility list and the required documentation.
Separately, PennDOT lets a Veteran add a Veterans designation to a standard driver license or to a commercial driver license.

PennDOT also offers military special registration plates, a military status endorsement for active duty members, a military CDL skills test waiver, and a process to register a vehicle in Pennsylvania while assigned out of state or deployed overseas.

PennDOT separately issues Severely Disabled Veteran parking placards. For those, the disability must be service-connected and certified by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs Regional Office Administrator in Philadelphia or Pittsburgh, and PennDOT accepts VA letters showing a 100 percent service-connected disability.
records.agency: PennDOT Driver and Vehicle Services

records.title: Veterans' preference in Pennsylvania public employment
records.summary: Pennsylvania adds 10 points to a Veteran's passing civil service examination score and requires appointing authorities to give preference to a qualified Veteran on the eligible list. The same preference extends to certain spouses and surviving spouses.
records.amount: 10 additional points added to a passing civil service examination score, which then sets the Veteran's standing on the eligible list
eligibility: Served in the armed forces of the United States, including a reserve component or the National Guard
Completed the initial contractual military service obligation
Last discharge or release was under conditions other than dishonorable
A member still on active duty may qualify within 90 days of an approved discharge after three or more years of service
Service is documented by a DD214, DD215, or NGB-22, or by a statement of service
A surviving spouse of a deceased service member, and the spouse of a Veteran the VA has classified as having a permanent total disability, receive the same preference
details: Two separate things happen. Section 7103 adds the 10 examination points for civil service appointments. Section 7104 requires an appointing authority filling a non-civil-service public position to give preference to a qualified Veteran.

The State Civil Service Commission states that appointing authorities must grant preference to a Veteran on the eligible list notwithstanding the Veteran's standing on that list, provided proper procedures are followed.
Section 7105 directs that military training and experience be counted as the equivalent of formal education when qualifications are assessed.
Chapter 71 also provides that age and a non-incapacitating physical impairment cannot disqualify an otherwise qualified Veteran, and that years of military service count toward seniority.
Chapter 71 is the exclusive Veterans' preference law for the Commonwealth, so it applies to Commonwealth and municipal public positions alike.
The Governor's Office of Administration handles preference questions at 717-783-6655 and ra-cs-vetpreference@pa.gov.
records.agency: Pennsylvania State Civil Service Commission and the Governor's Office of Administration
records.statuteRef: 51 Pa.C.S. Ch. 71 (sections 7101 to 7111), especially sections 7103, 7104, 7105, and 7108

records.title: Veterans' Temporary Assistance for a short-term financial emergency
records.summary: Pennsylvania offers a limited cash grant to a Veteran or an unmarried surviving spouse who temporarily cannot afford the necessities of life. It covers food, shelter, fuel, and clothing only, and it is meant for a documented immediate emergency.
records.amount: Up to $1,600 in a 12-month period, per DMVA. The statute itself sets no dollar figure. It caps assistance at the established maximum or the documented amount of need, whichever is less.
eligibility: Honorable discharge from the U.S. Armed Forces documented by a DD Form 214, or died in service or killed in action, or has a service-connected disability certified by the VA
Eligible applicants are the Veteran or the unmarried surviving spouse of a deceased Veteran
Bona fide Pennsylvania resident who does not maintain legal residence in another state
Temporarily unable to afford the necessities of life because of loss of income, assets, or support due to sickness, disability, unemployment, or natural or manmade disaster
Not receiving sufficient assistance from another state or federal agency
Must show a clear and present direct and immediate need
details: The grant is restricted to food, shelter, fuel, and clothing. It is not general-purpose cash.
The statute prohibits paying assistance in the form of relief orders, and lets the department scale amounts to the money available in the fund.
DMVA lists the supporting documents: DD Form 214, proof of residency, documentation of the loss of employment or income, proof of other benefits and income, and receipts for the expenses.
You apply through the County Director of Veterans Affairs in the county where you live. A denial can be appealed to the Adjutant General.
General questions go to Ra-vta@pa.gov. DMVA asks that completed applications and personal information not be emailed.
records.agency: Pennsylvania Department of Military and Veterans Affairs

records.title: Total property tax exemption on your home at a 100 percent rating
records.summary: A Veteran awarded 100 percent disability compensation with a rating of 100 percent disabled, or of individual unemployability, pays no property tax at all on the total appraised value of their residence homestead.
records.amount: The total appraised value of your residence homestead
eligibility: The VA has awarded you 100 percent disability compensation for a service-connected disability
And your rating is either 100 percent disabled or individual unemployability
The property must be your residence homestead as defined in Texas Tax Code Section 11.13
A surviving spouse may continue the exemption if the Veteran qualified at the time of death
details: Individual unemployability counts the same as a 100 percent schedular rating for this exemption. That catches a lot of Veterans who assume they do not qualify.
This is separate from and much larger than the partial exemption under Section 11.22. Check both.
Claimed through your county appraisal district, not the state.
records.agency: Texas county appraisal districts

records.title: Partial property tax exemption by disability rating
records.summary: Texas exempts part of the assessed value of a property you own on a sliding scale tied to your VA disability rating, from $5,000 at a 10 percent rating up to $12,000 at 70 percent or more.
records.amount: $5,000 to $12,000 of assessed value, by rating bracket
eligibility: 10 percent up to 30 percent rating: $5,000 of assessed value
30 percent up to 50 percent rating: $7,500
50 percent up to 70 percent rating: $10,000
70 percent and over: $12,000
You also get the full $12,000 if you are 65 or older with a rating of at least 10 percent, are totally blind in one or both eyes, or have lost the use of one or more limbs
A surviving spouse may be entitled to a portion of the exemption
details: You designate which property the exemption applies to. It does not have to be a homestead.
The age-65 provision matters: a 10 percent rating that is worth $5,000 before 65 is worth $12,000 after, which is a big jump that is easy to miss.
If you have a 100 percent rating or individual unemployability, look at the total homestead exemption under Section 11.131 instead, which is far larger.
records.agency: Texas county appraisal districts

records.title: Hazlewood Act tuition exemption
records.summary: Texas public colleges and universities must waive tuition and most required fees for qualifying Veterans, up to 150 credit hours. It is one of the most generous state education benefits in the country.
records.amount: Tuition and most required fees, up to 150 credit hours
eligibility: You currently reside in Texas
And you entered the service in Texas, declared Texas as your home of record, or would have been a Texas resident when you entered service
You were honorably discharged after more than 180 days of active duty, excluding training

You served during a qualifying period, which includes the national emergency that began September 11, 2001, the Persian Gulf War, Panama, Grenada and Lebanon, Vietnam, the Cold War, Korea, and both World Wars
